per_object_cap.stated: Sandboxes can be configured with 1 to 8 vCPUs and 1 to 8 GiB of RAM; the default sandbox has 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB. Storage is 10 GiB on Hobby.
per_object_cap.notes: The hard cap here is time, not shape: 1 hour of continuous runtime per session on Hobby. The billing docs' own cost advice gives the default as '2 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM', which contradicts the pricing page's 4 GiB.

interface_detail: SDK (Python, JavaScript) over a REST API; Sandbox.create() plus pause and resume
tooling: e2b Python and Node SDKs; templates; sandbox pause and resume
chaining: pause keeps memory, so a long agent run resumes mid-process rather than replaying its setup
limits_note: The 1-hour continuous runtime is the headline difference between Hobby and the USD 150 a month Pro plan, so the time cap is a plan gate rather than a technical ceiling. It resets on pause and resume.
reliability_note: A sandbox that hits the one-hour limit is destroyed and its in-memory state is lost unless it was paused or snapshotted first; the default timeout when none is set is 5 minutes.

free_tier.stated: Hobby is USD 0 a month with 'One-time $100 in usage credits', 'Up to 20 concurrently running sandboxes', 'Up to 1 hour per sandbox session', '10 GiB of sandbox storage, included' and 'No credit card required to start.'
free_tier.notes: The credit is one time and does not reset. Running sandboxes are billed per second on provisioned CPU and RAM.

retention.stated: Sandbox storage is included with every plan at no extra cost; a paused sandbox keeps its filesystem and its memory. 'Paused sandbox retention: Unlimited' on every plan.
retention.notes: a paused sandbox is kept indefinitely with no time-to-live and no automatic deletion; it is removed only when killed

egress.terms: No egress charge or allowance is stated on the pricing page; sandbox storage is stated free and the page prices CPU and RAM only. Outbound traffic leaves from ephemeral rotating IPs with no published CIDR list.

notes: Arithmetic, recomputed today: 2 vCPU x USD 0.0504 + 4 GiB x USD 0.0162 + 0 storage = USD 0.1656 an hour. USD 100 / 0.1656 = 603.9 h = 25.2 days at 24/7, and a 730-hour month would cost USD 120.89. But those 604 hours cannot be taken as a continuous machine: Hobby caps continuous runtime at 1 hour, so they are 604 sessions of one hour or less, and the credit is the smaller constraint only in the sense that it runs out second. At the maximum shape, 8 vCPU / 8 GiB, the hour is USD 0.5328 and USD 100 buys 187.7 h = 7.8 days, still in one-hour slices. GPU trap: not applicable, because E2B states it sells no GPU at all, so there is no advertised product the credit fails to cover. The real catch is the card AFTER the credit, not before: 'If you have no payment method, every project in your workspace is blocked shortly afterwards. Add a payment method to continue using E2B.' That is a hard stop at the end of the USD 100 with no free path onward. Pausing is unlimited and free, so a paused sandbox can sit indefinitely, but it is not running. One conflict to note: the billing docs' cost advice says the default is '2 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM' while the pricing page says 4 GiB; if 512 MiB is right the hour is USD 0.1089 and the credit buys 918 h, so the shape should be checked in the console before trusting either figure.
